A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities and countries that work together to deliver websites, videos, and images faster. Without one, every request for a webpage has to travel all the way back to a single origin server — the original computer where the website's files are permanently stored. If that server is far away, loading takes longer, and if many people request the same content at once, the server can slow down or struggle to keep up.

A CDN solves this by placing copies of popular content on many smaller computers positioned close to where people are. Each of these nearby computers is called an edge location, since it sits at the "edge" of the network, near the end user rather than at the distant center. When a request arrives, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy of the requested content. If it does, that's called a cache hit, meaning the content can be delivered immediately without contacting the original server at all. Think of it like a chain of local bakeries that keep fresh bread on hand nearby, so customers do not need to travel to a single distant factory every time they want a loaf. Only when no nearby copy exists does the request travel back to the origin server, after which the edge location saves a copy for next time. This arrangement makes websites load faster, reduces strain on the original server, and keeps services working smoothly during high demand.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer where a website's files are permanently kept | It is the ultimate source of truth, but relying on it alone for everyone is slow and fragile |
| Edge location | A smaller computer positioned near end users, far from the origin server | Nearby copies mean shorter travel time for requests, so pages appear more quickly |
| Cache hit | When a nearby edge location already has a saved copy of the requested content | It avoids a long trip to the origin server, speeding up delivery and reducing load |
| Latency | The delay between asking for content and receiving it | Lower latency means a smoother, faster experience, which a CDN is built to achieve |
